title: Netlify Pricing: Free Plan, Limits and Costs (2026)
summary: Netlify pricing extends beyond tier costs, with additional charges for usage and features. Understand what adds up on your bill for each plan.
body_markdown:
## Netlify deploy and usage alerts with Activepieces


Activepieces won't lower your Netlify bill, but it can show you what's driving it, so you can cut costs strategically.


Its core is MIT-licensed, and its 742 integrations are counted straight from the public GitHub monorepo, which has 25,126 stars, with roughly 60% contributed by the community, which means the numbers are openly auditable.


If the connector you need for a Netlify event isn't there, you don't wait on a vendor's roadmap: Activepieces can build the missing integration with AI, and it stays private to your own instance.


Netlify's webhooks and API can feed failed-deploy and usage alerts into Slack or email and log usage to a sheet.


Activepieces allows unlimited flows on every plan, and each flow is a trigger followed by actions. Credits meter AI usage, and Bring-Your-Own-Key moves model spend to your own provider bill.


That's the same shape as the one in the screenshot below, where a Stripe "Payment Failed" trigger feeds a Slack "Send Message To A Channel" action and the run detail shows the step completed.


The screenshot shows a two-step flow completing, which is the whole pattern. Swap Stripe for a Netlify event and you'll have a failed-build alert in a channel your team already reads.


What follows is what the flow does for each kind of reader. It monitors spend. It doesn't change the price or choose a plan for you.


For a personal or hobby site, one flow is enough: a failed-deploy message to your email or a Slack channel. You aren't trying to control a bill here, only to avoid finding out days later that a build broke.


Because you can see every run, you also learn how often you deploy, and that's the number to compare against any plan's build allowance.


Builds and seats are where the bill grows for this team, so log them. Send each deploy event to a sheet, with a row per build, and review it monthly.


Your own build count then replaces a guess, and you can check it against the tier you're considering before a seat or an extra build minute surprises you.


A failed-deploy alert to the team channel also stops people re-running broken builds, which wastes metered build time.


### Netlify usage alerts for high-traffic production sites


Usage is the line item that moves here. Poll Netlify's API on a schedule and write bandwidth and request figures to the sheet, then alert when a reading crosses a threshold you set.


You get a warning mid-cycle instead of an invoice afterward. The limit is that you choose the threshold, so set it from your own traffic history, not from a plan's headline allowance.
